newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council backs peace talks; concern for refugees.
newsitem.headline: UN Council backs peace talks; concern for refugees.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council, at the request of the United States, welcomed the anticipated Zaire peace talks and called on rebels to treat Rwandan refugees properly and allow investigations into reported massacres.

In a statement read at a formal meeting late on Wednesday, the council greeted the agreement by Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila to "discuss a peaceful and negotiated settlement of the conflict in Zaire" on a specified date and venue.

Diplomats said the United States called the meeting at the request of Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations who is currently in Zaire, so commitments made to him orally could be put in writing.

Aides to Mobutu said the president would fly to Gabon on Thursday before the meeting with Kabila on a South African navy ship in international waters in the Atlantic on Friday. Mobutu had raised last minute objections on the venue.
Some diplomats said it was possible Kabila or Mobutu would board the ship near Luanda, Angola, rather than Gabon, if the meeting takes place.

The council noted Kabila's promise to allow humanitarian agencies access to the Rwandan refugees and repatriate them by using both airports in Kisangani. It also noted his commitment to be flexible, a reference to his not holding aid agencies to the 60-day repatriation deadline he had set.

The 15-member body called on the rebel Alliance of Democratic Force for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire (ADFL) "to abide by these commitments and to enable the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees' repatriation plan to be implemented without conditions or delay."

The council also said it was deeply concerned about continuing reports of massacres and other atrocities in eastern Zaire of Rwandans. And it reminded the rebels to cooperate fully with U.N. investigations "by ensuring unimpeded access to all areas and sites under investigation as well as the securty of the members of the mission."

"It (the council) attaches great importance to the commitment of the leader of the ADFL to take appropriate action against members of the ADFL who violate the rules of international humanitarian law concerning the treatment of refugees and civilians," the statement said.

Meanwhile Kabila's aides said the face-to-face meeting, arranged by South Africa and the United Nations, should concern itself mainly with Mobutu's permanent retirement from his 32-year-old reign over Zaire. But there was no indication Mobutu had agreed to step down.
Richardson did not persuade Kabila to accept a ceasefire ahead of the talks or make any commitment to accept a transitional government before elections.

These are the key components of a peace plan drawn up by the U.N. special envoy, Mohamed Sahnoun, who will attend the talks at sea. The council late on Wednesday reiterated its support of the Sahnoun plan.
The rebels have begun to move huge numbers of refugees to Kisangani by night, swiftly threatening to overwhelm United Nations aid facilities set up to airlift them home.
Over 200 refugees left Kisangani by air for Rwanda's capital Kigali on Wednesday, the first since the rebels gave the go-ahead on Sunday for the repatriation to begin.
More than 100,000 refugees fled into dense forest surrounding the camps, but have slowly been making their way back, driven by hunger, exhaustion and illness.

The rebels under Kabila have captured most of Zaire. They are allied with Rwanda's Tutsi-led government, while most of the refugees are Hutus who fled after massacres in mid-1994 in which Hutu militants killed more than half a million Tutsis.
Among the refugees were militia who instigated the massacres, but many are considered innocent of the killings.
